set.venue: NewSum 2023 — 4th New Frontiers in Summarization Workshop (peer-reviewed workshop)
set.content: Chain-of-Density produces a summary through successive rewrites at a fixed length. The model writes an initial sparse summary, then repeatedly identifies salient entities missing from it and rewrites to include them without increasing the length, which forces compression: filler gives way to named entities and specifics. Adams et al. evaluated this on CNN/DailyMail news articles using GPT-4, and reported that human annotators preferred the denser intermediate steps over the sparse first pass — though preference fell away at the highest densities, where summaries became harder to read. Two scope caveats matter. The study used one model on one news-summarization dataset, so transfer to long reports, meeting transcripts or technical documents is plausible but unevidenced. And it was published at a peer-reviewed workshop (NewSum 2023) rather than a main conference. The mechanism is still a sound and cheap way to raise information density when a length ceiling is fixed; just treat the optimum number of rounds as something to tune, not as a published constant.

set.summary: Generic personas do not reliably improve factual accuracy; irrelevant persona detail can actively hurt.
set.best_for: Deciding whether a role or persona line is worth adding — and keeping any persona relevant and minimal.
set.limitations: Generic personas did not reliably improve factual accuracy across 4 model families and 162 roles, and the best persona per question could not be predicted better than chance. Irrelevant persona detail can cause large accuracy drops; mitigations helped only the largest models. Any benefit is mainly stylistic.
set.content: Assigning the model a role is one of the most common prompt moves and one of the least reliably beneficial. The strongest evidence concerns the generic version: Zheng et al. tested 162 role descriptions across four model families on 2,410 factual questions and found that adding a persona to the system prompt did not reliably improve accuracy over no persona at all, with the effect of a given persona close to random. Choosing the best persona for each question after the fact did help, but predicting that persona automatically performed no better than chance, so the benefit cannot be captured by a fixed role label. Luz de Araujo et al., across nine models and 27 tasks, found expert personas mostly neutral-to-positive, but showed that irrelevant persona details, such as biographical padding unrelated to the task, can cause large accuracy drops, and that mitigations helped only the largest models. The practical reading: a generic label such as 'You are a senior developer' should not be expected to improve factual correctness. If a persona is used to steer tone, vocabulary or framing, keep it directly relevant to the task and free of irrelevant detail.
